title: Salvage fridges and air conditioners without opening the refrigerant
summary: Fridges, freezers, air conditioners and dehumidifiers hold refrigerant in a sealed loop. Recovering it properly needs training and a recovery machine you almost certainly won't have. This guide shows how to take the useful parts without opening the loop, and what to do if the loop is already broken.

materials.item: Resistor discharge tool for run capacitors

steps.text: First decide whether the whole unit is worth more working. A fridge or air conditioner that still runs is worth moving whole on a hand truck.

Unplug it. Find the rating plate (inside the fridge door, on the back, or on the side of an AC unit) and read the refrigerant type. R-600a and R-290 burn. R-134a, R-410A, R-22 and R-12 don't burn but are under pressure.
steps.warn: Flammable refrigerants can ignite from a spark or flame if a line breaks. Treat them like propane.

steps.text: Learn the sealed loop by sight: the black dome compressor, the condenser coil (a black grid on the back of a fridge, or a finned coil in an AC unit), the evaporator in the cold part, and the copper or aluminium tubes joining them, including a very thin capillary tube. Everything else you can take.
Before touching wiring, discharge the run or start capacitor near the compressor and the fan motors with the resistor tool, then check it with your meter.
steps.warn: Run capacitors can hold a mains-level charge after unplugging.

steps.text: Take the parts outside the loop: fans and fan motors, wiring, relays, thermostats and timers, lights, door switches, glass shelves, magnetic door seals, control boards and sheet metal.
You can unclip the compressor's electrical cover and take the start relay and overload, but leave the compressor and its tubes alone.
Work around tubes, never through them. If a tube is in the way of a part, leave that part.
steps.warn: Don't bend, kink or lever against tubing. A nicked tube can split and spray.

steps.text: If the loop is already broken (a snapped or cut tube, a smashed unit), the gas has already escaped. Air the area out for a few minutes and keep flames away. Then you can unbolt the compressor and coils.
steps.warn: The oil in a compressor still holds some refrigerant. No torches or grinders on the tubes.

steps.text: If you need a compressor or coils, look for a unit whose loop is already broken. Never cut, drill, unbraze or heat tubes on an intact system.
A dead fridge or chest freezer with its loop left intact still makes an excellent insulated box for storage, or a cool store dug into the ground.

notes:
## Why not just cut the line

- **Frostbite.** Liquid refrigerant boils far below freezing as it escapes (R-134a at about −26 °C, R-410A at about −50 °C). The spray freezes skin and eyes instantly.
- **No air.** In a small room a big leak pushes out the air. You won't smell it.
- **Fire.** Many modern fridges and some AC units use isobutane (R-600a) or propane (R-290). The charge is small but can flash in a closed room.
- **Toxic smoke.** Heat from a torch or fire can break most other refrigerants down into very toxic gases, including hydrogen fluoride.
- **Damage beyond you.** Many refrigerants are strong greenhouse gases, and older ones (R-12, R-22) damage the ozone layer.

## What proper recovery needs

Training, a refrigerant recovery machine, a rated recovery cylinder, gauges, valves or piercing tools, and scales. If you don't have every one of these, don't attempt it. Leave the sealed system alone.

## What's worth taking

| Part | Where | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Fan motors | Behind the back panel, beside the compressor, in the freezer | Ventilation, small drives |
| Thermostat, relays, timers | Control box or inside the cabinet | Controlling heaters, coolers and pumps |
| Door seals | Around the door | Magnetic strips and seals |
| Glass shelves | Inside | Toughened glass for solar ovens and dehydrators |
| Sheet metal and wiring | Case and harness | Building material, wire |
| The cabinet itself | Whole unit | Insulated storage box |

## Common mistakes

- Cutting the thin capillary tube "just to let it out".
- Using a grinder near tubing to get a part out faster.
- Opening an intact system in a basement or small kitchen.
- Forgetting the run capacitor before grabbing the wiring.
